title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
hook: a refrain that never changes, and a list that slips in hunger, sleep and error beside peace and compassion

segments.voice: Yesterday: Govinda jaya jaya, Krishna's names sung like a call. The names are already doing the calling.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `GOVINDA JAYA JAYA, NAMES AS A CALL.`

segments.voice: Halfway through the evening, the music changes key and the room turns toward the Goddess. The leader begins a verse with the same ending every time, a run of bows the whole room picks up almost at once. Only one word in the middle changes. Peace. Faith. Compassion. Mother. Words that sound right for a hymn to a goddess. But stay for the whole list, and other words come round too, words nobody would put on a greeting card. Hunger. Sleep. Thirst. And, near the end, error.
screen: `THE ROOM TURNS TO THE GODDESS.` → `ONE WORD CHANGES EACH TIME.` → `PEACE, FAITH ... HUNGER, ERROR.`

segments.voice: The song comes from the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a text set inside the Markandeya Purana. In its fifth chapter the gods, driven from heaven, go to the Himalaya and praise her. The verse they repeat goes like this in Sanskrit: ya devi sarva-bhuteshu, then a quality, rupena samsthita, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namo namah. In paraphrase: to the Goddess who dwells in all beings in the form of this, bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, bow, bow. Then the gods fill in the blank, verse after verse. Consciousness. Intelligence. Sleep. Hunger. Shadow. Power. Thirst. Patience. Modesty. Peace. Faith. Loveliness. Fortune. Memory. Compassion. Contentment. Mother. And error, the word bhranti, confusion, mistaking one thing for another. So the hymn finds her not only in the parts of life that look holy, but in the tired body asking for sleep, the stomach asking for food, even the mind that gets things wrong. For Shaktas, Hindus who honor the Goddess as the highest, this is close to the heart of the matter: she is the power moving through everything, the plain and the bright alike. Sung as kirtan, the bow at the end never changes, so even someone with no Sanskrit can join from the second verse. The changing word is the leader's job. The room's job is to keep bowing, whatever word comes up.
screen: `FROM THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `TO THE GODDESS IN ALL BEINGS.` · `IN SLEEP, HUNGER, EVEN ERROR.` · `THE BOW NEVER CHANGES.` · then, large: `WHATEVER COMES UP, BOW.`

segments.voice: Check in with the body from the stomach up and name what's here, plainly, one word at a time: hunger, tiredness, thirst, restlessness. Then name something brighter that's also here, a little patience, a memory, some contentment, without ranking them, letting each word come and go like the changing word in the hymn. If you pray, follow each word with the hymn's refrain, said silently; if not, notice that both kinds of word belong to the same life.
Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: ya devi sarva-bhuteshu, to the Goddess in all beings, found in peace and compassion, and in hunger, sleep and error too.
Your line: Hunger, bow. Error, bow. Day nine hundred ninety-one, and the Goddess's song is done.

howItsDone: The ya devi sarva-bhuteshu verses are recited and sung in Goddess worship, especially during Navaratri, and at kirtans the room often joins the unchanging bow while a leader sings the changing word.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn to a goddess praises only beautiful things.
what it means: this hymn bows to the Goddess in all beings, in hunger, sleep and error as well as peace and compassion.

chat.says: Why would a hymn to the Goddess mention hunger, and even error?
options: It bows to her in all beings: in hunger, sleep and error, as well as peace.
It's a warning: those are the demons the gods were fighting in the story.
Those words are curses, sung so the Goddess will send them to enemies.
chat.meaning: In Devi Mahatmya chapter five, the gods bow to the Goddess dwelling in all beings, naming hunger, sleep and error alongside peace and compassion.
